title: Jev: a boring classifier that unlocks a lot
summary: Jev is a classifier: it picks an answer from a list. That sounds boring. But it is fast, cheap and accurate at the same time, and that opens up new uses.…
body_markdown:
**Research note**


**19,118** real moments tested


**36,218** Jev calls


September 2026


The short version


- **Jev is a classifier.** You give it some text and a list of possible answers. It picks one, and tells you how sure it is.
- **That sounds boring.** Classifiers have been around for decades: spam filters, fraud flags, ticket routing.
- **The twist.** Old classifiers were fast and cheap but not very smart. Big AI models are smart but slow and expensive. Jev is fast, cheap and smart at the same time.
- **Why that matters.** Any decision that has to be made thousands of times, in a fraction of a second, can now use real understanding.
- **On our own data.** We tested Jev against rule based guardrails and against LLM based guardrails, on the same 469 test cases. When it decides, Jev makes 3.8x to 7.5x fewer mistakes than an LLM judge, answers about 9x faster, and costs 79x to 214x less.


## 1


What is Jev?


Jev is an AI model released by TypeSafe on 15 September 2026. It does exactly one job:


- **It reads a situation.** Any text: an email, a web page, a price feed, a conversation.
- **It answers questions about it.** Each question comes with its own fixed set of possible answers.
- **It says how sure it is.** Every answer comes with numbers that show its confidence.


### A classifier, in one minute


A **classifier** is a program that sorts things into boxes. You have used many without noticing:


- **Your spam filter** sorts email into "spam" and "not spam".
- **Your bank** sorts card payments into "normal" and "suspicious".
- **A help desk** sorts tickets into "billing", "technical" and "sales".


Jev is a classifier too. Here are questions it can answer:


- "Is this email urgent?" → yes or no.
- "Which button should the robot click next?" → A, B or C.
- "How frustrated is this customer?" → calm, annoyed or angry.


### So why is it a big deal?


Until now, you had to choose between two kinds of tool.


Table 1 · The old trade off, and where Jev sits Classic classifier Big AI model (chatbot style) Jev


Understands messy language Poorly Well Well


Speed per answer Very fast Seconds Fraction of a second


Cost per answer Almost free Adds up fast Almost free


Needs training data first Yes, lots No No, you write the question


That last column is the point. Jev gives you the understanding of a big model at the speed and price of a small one.


**So what?** Every place where a decision was too frequent, too fast or too cheap to justify a big model can now get real understanding. That is a lot of places: every click of a browser agent, every trade, every safety check on every action.


## 2


How it works


Every call to Jev has two parts:


- **The state.** The text describing the situation.
- **The questions.** What you want to know, each with its possible answers written out.


### The three kinds of question


Table 2 · Jev's three question types Type What it asks Example What comes back


Choice Which option fits best? Which team handles this ticket: billing, technical or sales? The option picked, a probability for every option, and a confidence


Score Where does this sit on my scale? How frustrated is the customer, from calm to very angry? A position on your scale (up to 10 steps), and a confidence


Noul Is this statement true? The message sounds urgent. One number from 0 (surely false) to 1 (surely true)


### A real example


This is the example from TypeSafe's own quickstart.1 The state is a customer message:


> "Hi, I've been trying to connect my Stripe account for 3 days and it keeps failing. I'm losing sales. Please help ASAP."


Three questions are asked about it, all at once. Jev answers:


- **Department (Choice):** "technical", with a probability of 0.84. Billing got 0.159, sales 0.001.
- **Frustration (Score):** 1.035 on a scale from 0 (calm) to 2 (very angry). So: "frustrated but civil".
- **Urgent? (Noul):** 0.999. Almost certainly urgent.


The raw answer looks like this. No sentences to read, just values your software can use directly:


```text
{
"department": {
"choice": "technical",
"probabilities": { "billing": 0.159, "technical": 0.84, "sales": 0.001 },
"confidence": 0.596
},
"frustration": { "score": 1.035, "confidence": 0.842 },
"is_urgent": { "noul": 0.999 }
}


```


### What "how sure" means


Probability and confidence are what make Jev safe to use in real software.


- **Probability** says how likely each answer is. Above, "technical" was 0.84: likely, not certain.
- **Confidence** summarises how clear cut the whole question was. TypeSafe computes it from the spread of the probabilities.2
- **Calibration** means the numbers are honest on average. If Jev says "90% sure" on 100 different questions, about 90 of those answers should be right.
- **The catch:** that holds over many answers, not for any single one. TypeSafe says so plainly: it "does not guarantee that an individual answer is correct."2


So the usual pattern, which TypeSafe recommends and we use, is:


- **High confidence:** act automatically.
- **Medium confidence:** act, but carefully (for example, only warn).
- **Low confidence:** do not act. Hand it to a person or a simpler rule.


**So what?** You never have to trust Jev blindly. You choose how sure it must be before it acts, and everything below that bar goes to a safer path. The cost of a wrong answer, not the model, sets the bar.


### Many questions, one call


- **You can ask many questions in one call.** Jev answers each one separately, as if it were the only question, and all at the same time.
- **So adding questions barely slows it down.** In TypeSafe's own test, one call with 13 questions was 12.2 times cheaper and 10 times faster than 13 separate calls, with the same answers.3
- **This changes how you design.** Instead of one big vague question ("Is this reply good?"), you ask five small sharp ones ("Is it in the user's language?", "Does it make a promise?", and so on). Then your own code combines the answers.


## 3


Why it is different


To see why Jev is fast, you need to know how chatbot style models answer.


### How a chatbot style model answers


- **It works with tokens.** A token is a small piece of a word. "Unbelievable" might be three tokens: "un", "believ", "able".
- **It writes one token at a time.** Each new token needs a full pass through the model, and it cannot start the next one until the last is done.
- **Even a one word answer is written.** To answer "yes", the model still reads your whole question, then writes. Often it writes an explanation first, because you asked for one or because it "thinks" before answering.
- **Then your software has to read the text.** It must find the answer inside the sentence and hope it is spelled the way you expected.


### How Jev answers


- **It never writes.** TypeSafe describes its engine as producing "all outputs in a single query".4
- **The answer is already a value.** A choice from your list, a position on your scale, or a number. Nothing to parse.


### What that gets you


According to TypeSafe:4


- **Speed.** 70 to 500 milliseconds per call (a millisecond is a thousandth of a second). TypeSafe puts this at 40 to 200 times faster than big models on the same kind of question, and says its best numbers sit "on the higher end of real world gains".
- **Price.** $0.042 per million tokens of input. The answers themselves are free. On its own demo, TypeSafe measured 444.6 times cheaper than big models. It also admits it "can't prove it isn't subsidized" yet.
- **No made up answers.** An AI "hallucination" is when a model confidently invents something: a fact, a name, an option that does not exist. Jev can only return one of the answers you listed, so it cannot invent a new one. TypeSafe calls this "zero hallucinations", and says openly that this is a guarantee of the format, "not empirical".


One thing it does **not** mean: Jev can still pick the **wrong** option from your list. That is exactly why the confidence numbers exist.


## 4


How it was made


TypeSafe says Jev needed three new pieces:4


- **A new model design** (architecture), built for deciding, not writing.
- **A new sampler** , the part that turns the model's calculations into answers. Jev's produces all answers at once.
- **A new training method** , called RLCD.


### The training method, from zero


Modern AI models are shaped by "reinforcement learning": the model tries, gets a reward or a penalty, and adjusts. TypeSafe describes three generations:5


- **RLHF, learning from human feedback.** People rate answers; the model learns to please them. This produced chatbots. The downside, per TypeSafe: it can reward "confident-sounding hallucinations", because a confident answer pleases people.
- **RLVR, learning from verifiable rewards.** The model is rewarded when its answer can be checked as correct, like a maths result. This produced reasoning models, which are smarter but "slower and more expensive".
- **RLCD, learning for calibrated decisions.** The model is rewarded for picking the right answer **and** for giving honest confidence numbers. It never writes text. This produced Jev.


### Who is behind it


- **The founder:** Diogo Almeida. TypeSafe credits Almeida as a co inventor of RLHF, the method behind modern chatbots.5 The launch post opens: "At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful."4
- **The name:** Jev belongs to a family TypeSafe calls System One, after the book *Thinking, Fast and Slow* . "System 1" is your fast, intuitive judgment, the kind you use to spot a face or feel that something is off. That is the job Jev is built for.


## 5


What people built in 48 hours


Within two days of launch, builders had put Jev into five very different products. Each one needs the same thing: **a decision, made again and again, faster than a big model can manage.**


### 5.1 A robot that uses websites


**Figure 1.** A browser agent that finds flights in about 7 seconds. Image: Gregor Zunic (@gregpr07) on X


- **Who:** Gregor Zunic, co founder of Browser Use, a company that makes AI agents which use websites like a person would.6
- **The problem:** a web agent makes a decision on every page: where to click, what to open. With a big model, each decision takes seconds, so a simple task takes minutes.
- **Where Jev fits:** on each page, the page content is the state and the clickable actions are the options. Jev picks the next action. A small writing model steps in only when text must be typed, because Jev cannot write.
- **The reported result:** a flight search done in 7 seconds, for $0.0039, with the video playing at normal speed.


### 5.2 An AI that plays Doom


**Figure 2.** Each frame becomes a state; the answers move the player. Image: Ziwen (@ziwenxu_) on X


- **What:** a demo of Jev playing the classic video game Doom, live.7
- **The problem:** a game moves on every fraction of a second. A player that thinks for two seconds is already dead.
- **Where Jev fits:** the game situation is described as text. Jev answers questions like "Should the player's trigger be held down right now?", with a bar for each possible answer, and the answers steer the player.
- **Why people noticed:** Ziwen, sharing the demo, estimated that 10 calls a second for an hour, 36,000 calls, would cost around 7 dollars. "Anything that has to keep up with a person was off the table before this."


### 5.3 Sorting a thousand research papers


**Figure 3.** 1,018 papers sorted into 24 topics for $0.08. Image: Hassan (@nutlope) on X


- **Who:** Hassan, who built 1kpapers.com.8
- **The problem:** 1,018 AI research papers needed to be grouped into topics so people can browse them.
- **The pipeline:**


- A writing model (DeepSeek V4 Flash) writes a short summary of each paper.
- Jev reads the title and summary and picks one of 24 topics.
- The site shows the papers by topic.


- **The result:** summaries cost $3.99. Classification cost $0.08 in total, with a typical (median) wait of 256 milliseconds per paper.
- **The lesson Hassan draws:** use "different models for different parts of the workflow, instead of using one model for everything." Hassan is still checking Jev's labels before switching the live site over.


### 5.4 A trading bot


**Figure 4.** One buy or sell decision per 300 ms block. Image: Jarrod Watts (@jarrodwatts) on X


- **Who:** Jarrod Watts.9
- **The problem:** on the Monad blockchain, a new block (a batch of trades) is produced every 300 milliseconds. A decision that arrives later misses the block.
- **Where Jev fits:** on every block, the latest prices are the state and the question is "buy or sell?". The screen shows each decision with its confidence and response time, between 79 and 171 milliseconds in the frame shown.
- **Note:** this is a demo, not trading advice.


### 5.5 Picking the right AI for each request


**Figure 5.** Each model gets one plain sentence; Jev picks. Image: eve (@eve) on X


- **Who:** eve.10
- **The problem:** some requests need a powerful, expensive model; others are simple and should go to a cheap, fast one. Something has to decide, instantly, for every request.
- **Where Jev fits:** each model is described in one plain sentence, for example "Complex reasoning and engineering tasks" and "Routine tasks where speed matters". Jev reads the request and picks the model. It is a Choice question.


## 6


Our case: guardrails for AI agents


### The setup


- **We run AI agents that do real work** : they read files, run commands, write plans and build things, over many steps.
- **Around those agents we run safety checks** , technically called **hooks** or guardrails. A hook is a small program that runs automatically at a fixed moment: when the user sends a message, before the agent uses a tool, or when the agent finishes a turn.
- **Each hook asks one question.** If the answer is bad, it blocks the action or nudges the agent to fix it.


### What the hooks ask


Some examples, in plain words:


- **When the user writes:** Is this new work that needs tracking, or just a thank you?
- **Before an action:** How risky is this action? Is this ticket a duplicate?
- **When a task is closed:** Does the proof actually match what "done" was supposed to mean?
- **When the agent replies:** Is the reply plain enough? Is it in the user's language? Did it promise something without doing it?


### The problem with today's hooks


Most of these hooks are **fixed rules** today: they count words, look for keywords, measure length.


- **They are fast and free.** They run in milliseconds and cost nothing.
- **But the questions are about meaning.** A rule that measures message length cannot tell a new request from a long thank you.
- **So they make two kinds of mistake:**


- A **wrong alarm** blocks or nudges the agent for nothing, which wastes a whole turn.
- A **missed alarm** lets a real problem through.


A big AI model would understand the meaning. But a hook runs on every single action, and a check that adds seconds and cents to every step is not usable. Jev, in theory, is fast and cheap enough. So we tested it properly.


## 7


How we tested it


The goal was a result we would trust enough to switch the old rules off. Here is the method, step by step.


### 1. Collect real cases


- **19,118 real moments** from our agents' past work: user messages, tool calls, finished turns and task board changes.
- **Secrets removed first.** Passwords and keys were masked before anything was sent to Jev.


### 2. Write an answer key


For each check, we need the right answer for a sample of cases. That is called a **label** , and the full set is the **answer key** .


- **Two separate AI reviewers** labeled each case, following a written guide. Neither saw Jev's answer or the old rule's verdict. This is called **blind** labeling.
- **A third reviewer** settled every case where the first two disagreed.
- **The person who runs these agents** also labeled 923 user messages by hand. This is the strictest test we have.


### 3. Split the cases, like an exam


- **Tuning set.** The cases we used to improve each check's questions and settings.
- **Test set.** Cases kept aside and used only once per version, at the end. A check that did well only on the cases it was tuned on would be like a student who memorised last year's exam.
- **Split by conversation.** A conversation's cases all sit on the same side, so the test never contains a near copy of a tuning case.


### 4. Let Jev pass when unsure


- **Each check has a confidence bar.** Above it, Jev decides. Below it, Jev stays quiet and the old rule decides.
- **We count Jev's mistakes only where it decided.** The share of cases where it decided is called **coverage** .
- **Both numbers matter.** Zero mistakes means little if Jev almost never decides.


### 5. Respect real time limits


- **A hook cannot wait forever.** Any Jev answer slower than 3 seconds counts as "no answer", and the old rule decides, exactly as it would live.


## 8


Results


### 8.1 Jev vs rules vs an LLM judge


We ran three kinds of guardrail on exactly the same 469 test cases, with the same answer key:


- **Rule based:** today's fixed rules.
- **LLM based:** a small model (Claude Haiku 4.5) and a mid size model (Claude Sonnet 5), each given the same situation and the same questions, and asked for the same answers.
- **Jev:** deciding when it is sure, and handing the rest to the rules.


Table 3 · Same 469 test cases, six checks System Mistakes when it decides Decides on Total mistakes, with rules as fallback Typical answer time Cost per answer


Rules only 148 of 469 (31.6%) 100% 148 about 50 ms $0


Haiku 4.5 (small LLM) 47 of 342 (13.7%) 73% 99 6.0 s $0.0065


Sonnet 5 (mid size LLM) 22 of 316 (7.0%) 67% 92 6.3 s $0.0178


Jev 5 of 274 (1.8%) 58% 90 0.66 s $0.00008


What it shows:


- **When it decides, Jev is the most accurate.** 7.5x fewer mistakes than Haiku, 3.8x fewer than Sonnet, per decision.
- **Jev decides less often.** It passes 42% of cases to the rules; the LLMs pass 27% to 33%.
- **So the total is close.** With the rules catching what each one passes on, Jev ends at 90 mistakes, Sonnet at 92, Haiku at 99, and rules alone at 148.
- **Speed and cost are not close.** Jev answers about 9x faster at the median, and costs 79x less than Haiku and 214x less than Sonnet per answer.


**So what?** For the same safety, Jev is the only option cheap and fast enough to run on every single action. An LLM guardrail matches it on total mistakes, but at several seconds and up to 200 times the price per check. And because Jev's mistakes when it decides are so rare, every point of coverage we add turns straight into fewer total mistakes.


How we measured, briefly:


- **Same inputs.** Each LLM received exactly the text and questions Jev received, and its answers went through the same decision code.
- **Same scoring.** An answer outside the allowed options counted as a mistake. Haiku produced one; Sonnet and Jev none.
- **Honest timing.** LLM times include starting the command line tool; the models' own reported time was about 4 s, still 6x slower than Jev. Extended thinking was off, which makes the LLMs faster and cheaper than their defaults.
- **One tilt in Jev's favour.** Jev's "sure enough" bars were tuned on separate cases; the LLMs used the same bars untuned. That can lower their coverage, not their accuracy when they decide.

**Figure 6.** Same test cases for both. Old rules: 98 wrong alarms. Jev: 19 mistakes in 511 decisions. Tap a row for details.[Open full size ↗](https://agent.nexus/images/blog/jev-the-model-that-decides-accuracy.png)


How to read this chart:


- **Black bar:** wrong alarms raised by the old rule.
- **Striped bar:** problems the old rule missed.
- **Orange bar:** Jev's mistakes, out of the cases where it decided.


What it shows:


- **Overall:** the old rules raised 98 wrong alarms. Jev made 19 mistakes in 511 decisions, about 3.7%.
- **Best case, "Is this message new work?":** the old rule raised 21 wrong alarms and missed 6. Jev made 1 mistake in 38 decisions.
- **"Does the proof match the finish line?":** the old rule raised 14 wrong alarms and missed 34. Jev made 3 mistakes in 29 decisions.
- **"Is a promise left unbacked?":** the old rule missed 17. Jev made 75 decisions with no mistake.
- **Not ready yet:** "What kind of request is this?" (5 mistakes in 38) and "Who must act on this task?" (3 in 8). These stay on the old rule until they pass.


**So what?** Fewer wrong alarms means fewer wasted turns and less noise for the agent. Fewer missed alarms means more real problems caught. On most checks Jev does both at once, and the ones that fail simply stay on the old rule, so nothing gets worse.

- **Version 3** decided on 638 of them (69%) and was wrong on 9 (1.4%).

**So what?** A human agreed with Jev on more than 98% of the decisions it made, on messages Jev had never been tuned on. That is the number that decides whether we let it act on its own, and it is close.

What it shows:


- **Some checks sit bottom right.** They decide on most cases with few mistakes.
- **Some sit bottom left.** They are rarely wrong, but only because they rarely decide. The old rule still does most of their work.

**So what?** The more often Jev decides, the more the old rules can be switched off. A check at bottom right is ready to replace its rule. A check at bottom left is safe but useless until its coverage grows, and that is where the tuning work goes.

**Figure 9.** How long each Jev answer took. Tall bars on the left: most answers are quick. Measured from one laptop in Europe, often 8 questions at a time.[Open full size ↗](https://agent.nexus/images/blog/jev-the-model-that-decides-latency.png)


Two terms first:


- **Median:** half of all answers were faster than this, half slower.
- **95th percentile:** 95% of answers were faster than this.


What we measured, over 36,218 calls:


- **Median:** 0.68 seconds.
- **95th percentile:** 1.79 seconds.
- **Too slow:** 781 calls (2.2%) took longer than our 3 second limit. The old rule decided instead, and nobody waited.


Why this is slower than TypeSafe's 70 to 500 milliseconds:


- **Bigger questions.** Each call carried the full context of the conversation: the user's message, the agent's previous reply, the tools used, the task board and the rule being enforced.
- **Plain internet.** Calls went from one laptop in Europe, usually 8 at a time.
- **Cold connections.** Each call opened a new secure connection. Reusing one brought single calls down to between 0.23 and 0.35 seconds in our tests.


**So what?** Under a second is fast enough to sit in front of every action without the user noticing. A chatbot style model at several seconds per check is not. And the tail is handled: when a call is slow, the rule decides and nobody waits.

**Figure 10.** What one Jev answer costs, per check. Price from TypeSafe: $0.042 per million tokens in, answers free.[Open full size ↗](https://agent.nexus/images/blog/jev-the-model-that-decides-cost.png)


- **One Jev answer** cost between $0.00003 and $0.00054 in our tests. The difference comes from how much context each check sends: more text means more tokens.
- **One wasted agent turn** , caused by a wrong alarm, was measured at $0.007 to $0.034.
- **So one avoided wrong alarm pays for 12 to over 1,000 Jev answers** , depending on the check.


**So what?** Cost is not a reason to hold back. Even on the most expensive check, Jev only needs to prevent one wasted turn in twelve to pay for itself. On the cheapest, one in a thousand.


## 9


What we learned


- **Use a deciding model when you only need a decision.** Paying a model to write a paragraph that your code then throws away is waste, in time and in money.
- **Confidence is the real feature.** It is what makes AI safe to put in the path of every action: act when sure, fall back when not. The fallback is part of the design, not a failure of it.
- **Ask small, sharp questions.** Five narrow questions beat one broad one. Plain code combines them, and the logic stays easy to read and to fix.
- **Context helps, and it costs.** More context makes answers better on some checks and slower and pricier on all of them. We now measure every check with and without it, and keep it only where it helps.
- **A test is only as good as its answer key.** Several early "mistakes" turned out to be errors in the labels, not in Jev. Checking the key is part of the work.


## 10


The fine print


- **One company, one assistant.** These results come from our own agents' hooks. Other systems will have other questions.
- **Small test sets for some checks.** Several checks decided on fewer than 40 test cases. A rule of thumb: zero mistakes in n cases still allows an error rate of up to about 3 in n. Treat small numbers as early signals.
- **Some settings saw the test.** For a few checks, the confidence bar was raised after looking at test answers. The chart's details say which; those figures are not a fair test.
- **Mostly AI labels.** Apart from the 923 hand labeled messages, the answer key comes from AI reviewers. A human review of the hardest cases is still to come.
- **TypeSafe's numbers are TypeSafe's.** Section 3 quotes its own benchmark; we did not rerun it.
- **Community numbers are the builders' own.** Section 5 reports what each builder posted; we did not rerun their demos.
- **Prices can change.** TypeSafe says it cannot yet prove its price is not subsidized.

Answer key (labels)The correct answers for a set of test cases, used to score a check.Blind labelingWriting the answer key without seeing what the system being tested said.CalibrationWhen confidence numbers are honest on average: "90% sure" is right about 90% of the time.Choice, Score, NoulJev's three question types: pick an option, place on a scale, or give the probability that a statement is true.ClassifierA program that sorts things into boxes, like "spam" or "not spam".ConfidenceA number summarising how clear cut a question was for Jev.CoverageThe share of cases where Jev was sure enough to decide.HallucinationWhen an AI model confidently invents something that is not true or does not exist.HookA small program that runs automatically at a fixed moment around an AI assistant, and can block or nudge it.Median, 95th percentileHalf of the values are below the median; 95% are below the 95th percentile.MillisecondA thousandth of a second.StateThe text Jev reads: everything it needs to know about the situation.TokenA small piece of a word.
